Virginia Beach by the numbers

Where is Virginia Beach and how is the city laid out?

Virginia Beach sits on the Atlantic Ocean at the mouth of the Chesapeake Bay in the southeastern corner of Virginia. It is an independent city, so the same government that runs schools and police also bills property tax, and there is no separate county in the picture.

The city covers 497.5 square miles in total, but only 244.72 of those are land. The rest is water, which makes Virginia Beach the largest city in the state by total area. Average elevation is about 12 feet above sea level, and a large part of the city drains to the Chesapeake Bay through the Lynnhaven River and its tributaries. Norfolk is 19 miles to the west.

A line on the map called the Green Line separates the developed northern part of the city from the rural south. Land north of it is close to built out, which is why many sales here involve older houses in established subdivisions rather than new construction.

FactDetailSource
Total area497.5 square miles, 244.72 land and 252.78 waterCensus Bureau figures cited by Wikipedia
2020 census population459,470Wikipedia, citing the census
Housing units, 2020190,059, with 6.2% vacantWikipedia, citing the census
Real estate billsTwo installments, Dec. 5 and June 5City Treasurer
Assessment noticesMailed by March 1 each yearReal Estate Assessor

How did Virginia Beach become one city?

The resort town was incorporated in 1906, became a city in 1952, and merged with neighboring Princess Anne County in 1963 after voters in both places approved a referendum. Princess Anne County had existed since 1691, so the merger folded more than 250 years of rural county history into one jurisdiction.

The 1883 arrival of rail service to the coast started the resort. The completion of Virginia Beach Boulevard in 1922 opened the route for cars, and The Cavalier Hotel opened in 1927. After the merger the new city was divided into seven boroughs: Bayside, Blackwater, Kempsville, Lynnhaven, Princess Anne, Pungo, and Virginia Beach.

The assessor updates ownership records from deeds, wills, and plats recorded with the Clerk of the Circuit Court.

What do the Assessor and the Treasurer each do in Virginia Beach?

The Real Estate Assessor sets the value of the property, and the City Treasurer sends the bill and collects the money. A third office, the Commissioner of the Revenue, now handles the real estate exemption and freeze programs, according to the Treasurer's page.

Taxes are assessed for the city's fiscal year of July 1 through June 30 and are paid in arrears. If your mortgage company holds an escrow account, the bill goes to the lender. People without escrow receive the bill directly from the Treasurer, and a paid-off mortgage or a change of lender is something you should report so the bill reaches the right place.

  • Assessor questions and appeals: call 757-385-4601 and ask for an appraiser.
  • Board of Equalization: 757-385-6296 or BOE@vbgov.com.
  • Bankruptcy notation on a tax account: email VBBK4you@vbgov.com with the case number.
  • Exemption and freeze programs: ask the Commissioner of the Revenue.

The Treasurer's real estate page also links to a tax search and an open data portal for delinquent real estate.

When are Virginia Beach property taxes due and what if they are late?

Real estate tax is due in two installments, December 5 and June 5, and a due date that lands on a weekend or city holiday moves to the next business day. Partial and advance payments are accepted if you cannot pay a bill in full.

Payments received or postmarked after the grace period carry a penalty of 10% of the total tax or $10, whichever is greater, but never more than the bill plus interest. Interest runs at 9.6% per year. A pending reduction does not excuse the penalty.

Any payment the Treasurer receives is credited first to the most delinquent account, which follows Virginia Code 58.1-3913. If a refund is due after a reduction, the city first checks for other delinquent charges, and the refund takes about four weeks.

  • Late fee: 10% of the tax or $10, whichever is more.
  • Interest: 9.6% per year.
  • Refund timing: about four weeks.
  • Weekend or holiday due date: next business day.

What happens when Virginia Beach taxes stay unpaid for years?

The city can advertise the property and eventually sue to collect. Once taxes are delinquent by three years plus the current tax year, the Treasurer may publish a list of properties with the record owner's name, in a newspaper or online, and charges a $25 advertising fee.

If the taxes are still unpaid on June 30 of the current fiscal year, the account can go to a law firm, and attorney fees are added. A lien may be recorded with the Virginia Beach Circuit Court clerk, after which the city may collect by any legal means, including offering the property for sale.

How does a sale work when real estate tax is still owed on the house?

The unpaid tax is paid out of the sale proceeds at closing, because Virginia law gives the tax lien priority over every other lien or encumbrance on the real estate. Under Code 58.1-3340, that lien stays in place until the taxing authority actually receives payment, and the purchaser or trustee at a sale must see that the proceeds are applied to taxes and levies on the property.

The statute defines taxes and levies to include the penalties and interest. It also says the seller's liability for tax is prorated by contract, which is why the purchase agreement and the settlement statement matter. For the Virginia Beach fiscal year, the Treasurer states that proration is calculated daily from the full annual amount, and that the installment dates do not set separate tax periods.

The treasurer or other proper officer causes the lien to be released once it is paid.

The state also taxes the deed itself. Code 58.1-802 imposes a grantor tax of 50 cents for each $500 of consideration, paid by the seller unless the parties agree that the buyer pays some of it. The clerk must certify payment before a deed is admitted to record.

How do I challenge a Virginia Beach assessment?

Start with a phone call to the Assessor's office, then use the written steps if the answer does not satisfy you. The office says many concerns are settled without additional time and cost, and it recommends the call before any formal appeal.

  • Reassessment notices are mailed by March 1 of each year.
  • Request for Reappraisal: an informal review, accepted March through April 30 of each tax year.
  • Board of Equalization: appeals may be filed from March through June 30 of each tax year.
  • Only the owner or a duly authorized agent may discuss the valuation, and an agent needs an original signed letter of authorization or a notarized power of attorney.

The Board of Equalization has six members appointed by the Circuit Court, and each member must own an interest in real property. Its page refers to hearing appeals for the July 1, 2026 values.

What should a Virginia Beach seller know about flooding and weather?

Water is the main physical risk to a house here. The climate is humid subtropical, with average annual precipitation between 47 inches at the airport and more than 50 inches at Back Bay, and August is the wettest month at over 5.5 inches on average.

Hurricane Matthew's heavy rainfall flooded more than 2,000 homes and left some neighborhoods under standing water for days. After that storm, the city turned down several proposals to build in floodplains. Hurricane Isabel in 2003 is named as the exception to the city's usual position south of major storm tracks, and an EF-3 tornado struck the Great Neck neighborhood on April 30, 2023, with no injuries reported.

Buyers of older houses in low areas tend to ask about past water and drainage.

Which parts of the city and which employers shape the housing market?

Real estate, defense, and tourism are the three sectors that Wikipedia names as major for the Virginia Beach economy. Naval Air Station Oceana, a major Navy fighter jet base, sits inside the city, and homes near it live with the operating constraints that housing growth has placed on the base.

Other institutions based in the city include Regent University, the Christian Broadcasting Network, the U.S. headquarters of Stihl, and the Association for Research and Enlightenment. The Town Center opened in 2003 and the Convention Center in 2005, both built with city help that included tax increment financing districts.

Named communities include Alanton, Cape Henry, Great Neck Point, Green Run, Kempsville, Lynnhaven, Pungo, and Sandbridge. Each has its own mix of ages and conditions.

More questions about Virginia Beach, VA Property Tax Guide

How much is the Virginia Beach real estate tax bill due in December?

The amount depends on your assessment and the current city rate, so look up your own bill on the City Treasurer's website. We did not confirm a current rate on an opened page, so we do not quote one. The bill is due December 5, with the second installment due June 5.

What is the penalty for paying Virginia Beach real estate tax late?

The penalty is 10% of the total tax or $10, whichever is greater, up to the amount of the bill plus interest, and interest runs at 9.6% per year. A pending reduction does not excuse the penalty, according to the Treasurer.

Can I sell my Virginia Beach house if the property tax is delinquent?

Yes. The unpaid tax, penalty, and interest are paid from the sale proceeds at closing because the tax lien comes ahead of other liens under Code 58.1-3340. Request a payoff figure from the Treasurer before you close.

When can I appeal my Virginia Beach assessment?

You can request a reappraisal from the Assessor from March through April 30, and file with the Board of Equalization from March through June 30 of each tax year. The office suggests calling an appraiser at 757-385-4601 first.

Does the Virginia Beach Treasurer or the Assessor decide my value?

The Real Estate Assessor decides the assessment. The City Treasurer only bills and collects the tax, so assessment questions go to the Assessor and payment questions go to the Treasurer.

Who pays the Virginia grantor tax when a house sells?

By statute the seller, or whoever signs for the seller, pays the 50 cents per $500 grantor tax, although the buyer and seller may agree that the buyer covers some or all of it.

Alexandria by the numbers

Where is Alexandria, VA, and how is the city laid out?

Alexandria is an independent city on the west bank of the Potomac River, about 15.35 square miles in size, with Washington, D.C. to the northeast, Arlington County to the north and northwest, and Fairfax County to the south (Wikipedia). Elevation runs from sea level to 287 feet.

Because it is an independent city, Alexandria bills its own real estate tax and has no county government above it. The city's main neighborhoods give a sense of the housing mix:

  • Old Town, the historic core near the river
  • Del Ray and Potomac, the former town of Potomac
  • Carlyle and Eisenhower East
  • Rosemont, West End, Potomac Yard and Arlandria

The city had 159,467 residents in the 2020 census and a 2025 estimate of 160,662. Median household income was $124,593 in the 2024 American Community Survey estimate.

What is the history that still shapes Alexandria property?

Alexandria was founded in 1749, became a town in 1779 and was ceded to the District of Columbia in 1801 before returning to Virginia in 1847. It was chartered as a city in 1852 and became independent in 1870, and annexations in 1915, 1930 and 1952 expanded its borders.

The Old Town historic district, created in 1946, was the third in the country. That history is why many Alexandria houses are regulated by a review board, as the next section explains.

Do historic district rules affect selling an Alexandria house?

They can, because exterior work in a local historic district needs approval from the Board of Architectural Review. The city regulates two local districts, Old and Historic Alexandria and Parker-Gray, plus buildings designated as One Hundred-Year-Old Buildings (Historic Preservation page).

  • A Certificate of Appropriateness is required for new construction and exterior alterations visible from a public right of way.
  • A Permit to Demolish is needed to demolish or encapsulate more than 25 square feet of material, whether or not it is visible.
  • Interior work does not need board approval.
  • Staff can approve some projects administratively, usually in under five business days.

The city offers a Historic Preservation map viewer to check whether an address is in a district. Preservation staff can be reached at 703.746.3833 or Preservation@alexandriava.gov.

What drives the Alexandria economy?

The federal government is the largest force in the city's economy. The biggest employers named are the Pentagon's Mark Center, with about 8,000 workers, and the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, with about 6,000. Tourism passed $1 billion in visitor revenue in 2024.

Metro's Blue and Yellow lines serve the city, with stations at King Street-Old Town, Braddock Road, Eisenhower Avenue and Van Dorn Street, and a Potomac Yard station that opened in 2023. The city runs its own DASH bus system, and Interstates 95, 495 and 395 and US 1 pass through it.

Alexandria City Public Schools operates 12 elementary schools, two pre-K through 8 schools, two middle schools and Alexandria City High School, which has two campuses.

What did the 2026 Alexandria assessment show?

Alexandria's total tax base rose 3.41 percent for 2026, the fifteenth straight year of net increase, and residential assessments rose 4.40 percent overall. The figures come from the Office of Real Estate Assessments notice insert (2026 key dates insert).

Of residential properties, 63 percent went up, 8 percent went down and 29 percent stayed the same. Only sales completed before January 1, 2026 counted toward the assessed values.

What are the 2026 Alexandria tax dates in order?

The city's 2026 key-dates insert lists the full calendar, and the notice itself is not a bill. The calendar below uses the dates printed on that insert.

  • February 25: assessment notices mailed.
  • March 16: deadline to request an administrative review. The city says no exceptions will be made to appeal deadlines.
  • April 15: deadline for elderly and disabled tax relief applications.
  • April 29: City Council adopts the FY 2027 budget and sets the tax rate.
  • June 1: deadline to appeal to the Board of Equalization.
  • June 15: first-half payment due, even if a review or appeal is pending.
  • Early October: second-half bills mailed.
  • November 16: second-half payment due. November 15 falls on a Sunday in 2026.

To start a review, email realestate@alexandriava.gov or call 703.746.4168.

Does Alexandria offer tax relief for older or disabled owners?

Yes. Alexandria runs a real estate tax relief and deferral program for owners who are 65 or older or permanently and totally disabled. Completed applications or annual certifications are due to the Department of Finance by April 15 each year (program page).

  • Household net assets may not exceed $430,000, excluding the home, up to one acre of land and the related mortgage.
  • Household gross income counts the applicant, a spouse and other owners living in the home.
  • Late applications may be accepted until April 15 of the next year for good cause, such as a hospitalization or first-time filing.
  • Deferred taxes are repaid with interest when the property is conveyed or the owner dies. Relieved taxes are not repaid.

The city's phone line is 703.746.4800, option 6, and the email is taxrelief@alexandriava.gov. The page we opened did not show the income limit, so ask the office for the current figure.

The deferral matters in a sale. If you deferred tax, the repayment falls due when the house is conveyed, so ask for the balance at the start.

Does the Potomac flood Old Town properties?

Parts of Old Town flood during storm surge and some low inlets flood from the tide alone. A city analysis of Potomac gauge data from 2004 to 2021 found the river above Action Stage about 112 days a year and above Flood Stage about 16 days a year (city flood frequency memo).

The memo names King Street at Strand and Union, and Union Street from Prince to Thompsons Alley, among the areas that flooded in 2021. Anyone selling near the waterfront should expect buyers to ask about flood insurance and past water in the basement or garage.

What does a deed transfer cost in Alexandria?

Virginia's state recordation tax on a deed is 25 cents per $100, applied to the greater of the price or the most recent assessment (Va. Code 58.1-801). A separate grantor's tax is 50 cents per $500 (58.1-802), and it excludes the value of liens that stay on the property.

The title company will prepare a settlement statement that shows these charges and the property tax payoff. Local and other recording charges are not covered here, so ask the title company.

How do sellers with Alexandria tax due usually proceed?

An Alexandria seller with unpaid tax can sell, and the title company pays the balance from proceeds. Ask the Treasury Division for a payoff that includes any penalty, and confirm whether the half-year bill already issued has been paid.

This page is general information. The city offices and a Virginia attorney can confirm figures for your parcel.

When is Alexandria property tax due in 2026?

The first half is due June 15, 2026, and the second half is due November 16, 2026, because November 15 falls on a Sunday. The city says the first payment is due even if a review or appeal is pending.

How do I appeal my Alexandria assessment?

Request an administrative review by March 16, 2026, then appeal to the Board of Equalization by June 1 if you still disagree. Email realestate@alexandriava.gov or call 703.746.4168.

Does Alexandria have tax relief for seniors?

Yes. Owners 65 or older, or permanently and totally disabled, can apply by April 15 each year, with household net assets capped at $430,000 excluding the home and up to one acre. Call 703.746.4800, option 6.

Do I need approval to change the outside of a house in Old Town?

Usually yes, if the house is in a local historic district and the work is visible from a public right of way. The Board of Architectural Review issues a Certificate of Appropriateness, and interior work does not need it.

How much did Alexandria assessments rise in 2026?

The total tax base rose 3.41 percent and residential assessments rose 4.40 percent. The average single-family home was valued at $1,045,750 and the average condo at $460,185.

Norfolk by the numbers

Who bills and collects real estate tax in Norfolk?

Two city offices split the work. The Office of the City Assessor sets the value, and the City Treasurer sends the bills and collects the money. City Council decides the tax rate and the due dates each year when it finalizes the budget, according to the Treasurer's real estate tax page.

Norfolk collects on a fiscal year that runs July 1 to June 30. The Treasurer's page says the office bills more than 68,000 taxable parcels every quarter, and bills are mailed at least 30 days before the due date. The Treasurer also collects nuisance abatement liens that come over from Neighborhood Quality, and those carry a 30 day payment window.

We could not open a Norfolk page that states the current rate per $100 of value, so this guide does not quote one. Ask the Treasurer or the Assessor for the rate on your parcel before you work out a payoff.

When are Norfolk real estate tax payments due?

Norfolk bills real estate tax four times a year, with due dates on September 30, December 5, March 31 and June 5. A Norfolk owner who sells mid-year can therefore owe a payment that came due only weeks earlier.

Source: City of Norfolk Treasurer. The city sets these dates annually, so check the current bill if you are close to a deadline.

How do you appeal a Norfolk assessment?

Norfolk gives owners two routes, an informal review with an appraiser and a formal hearing before the Board of Review. The Assessor's appeal page lays out both.

  • Informal appeal: call 757-823-1343 to book a conference, in person or by phone, with an appraiser. The window opens when the April notice arrives and closes May 8, or the next business day if May 8 is a weekend.
  • Formal appeal: file with the Board of Review by the last business day of May. The page lists June 1, 2026 as the received or postmarked cutoff for that year.
  • Packet: one original plus five full sets of copies, and a separate application for each parcel.
  • Representatives: an agent needs an original letter of authorization on the owner's letterhead, dated in the same calendar year and notarized.

At the hearing you get five minutes to show that the value is above market or not uniform with comparable homes. Virginia law presumes the assessor is correct, and the taxpayer carries the burden of proof under Va. Code 58.1-3379. An appraisal submitted as evidence must be written for appeal purposes, and for the 2026 cycle the page asks for a July 1, 2026 value date using 2025 sales.

Where is Norfolk, and how does the water shape its housing?

Norfolk is an independent city in southeastern Virginia where the Elizabeth River meets the Chesapeake Bay. Wikipedia gives it 96.41 square miles in total, but only 53.28 of those are land, with 43.13 square miles of water. The city sits at an elevation of about 6.9 feet.

That low ground matters to anyone selling. The 2020 census counted 238,005 residents, and a 2025 estimate puts the figure near 231,013. Tidal flooding days rose from about five in 2000 to roughly 10 to 15 by 2020, and Hurricane Isabel in 2003 pushed a storm surge into the Midtown Tunnel. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers began a Coastal Storm Risk Management project after a 2019 study, and Wikipedia reports a March 2026 estimate of $6.1 billion with completion planned for 2037.

A seller who can hand over an existing elevation certificate or a flood zone letter has a ready answer when a buyer asks about flood risk.

How does flood zone status affect selling a Norfolk house?

Flood zone status can change what a buyer pays for insurance, so Norfolk publishes a property lookup. The city's Flood Zones page explains that zones come from FEMA's Flood Insurance Rate Map and are enforced through Article 3.9.7 of the city zoning ordinance and the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code.

The page also points owners to a site called Forerunner, where you can search a property, see flood data and find existing elevation certificates. It lists these zone types:

  • X: outside the 0.2 percent annual chance of flooding.
  • Shaded X: 0.2 percent annual chance, with depths under 1 foot in a 1 percent event.
  • AE, AH and AO: 1 percent annual chance areas, with AE carrying a mapped base flood elevation.
  • VE and LiMWA: coastal areas affected by wave action.

If your house sits in an AE zone, expect the buyer's lender to ask about flood coverage. Either way, the title company still needs the tax lien cleared.

Which Norfolk neighborhoods and employers do sellers hear about?

Norfolk's housing stock is spread across older waterfront neighborhoods and newer revitalized districts. Wikipedia names Ghent, Colonial Place, Larchmont, North Shore, Edgewater and Lafayette Shores among the popular residential areas, plus the historic Freemason district. Berkley, Willoughby Spit and Ocean View have long ties to the water.

The 2024 employer list on Wikipedia puts these names at the top:

  • U.S. Department of Defense, with Naval Station Norfolk described as the world's largest naval installation
  • Sentara Healthcare
  • Norfolk City Public Schools and the City of Norfolk
  • Old Dominion University and Children's Hospital of the King's Daughters

A Navy family that gets orders on short notice may not have time for a repair list, and an as-is sale is one way to handle that.

What happens to unpaid tax when a Norfolk house sells?

Unpaid tax is paid from the sale proceeds, because Virginia puts the tax lien ahead of every other lien. Va. Code 58.1-3340 says the purchaser, or the trustee in a foreclosure, must apply proceeds to taxes and levies assessed on the property, and the lien covers penalties and interest too. The treasurer then releases it.

The statute also says the seller's tax liability is prorated by contract, so the purchase agreement should state who covers the current quarter. Virginia adds a grantor's tax of 50 cents per $500 under Va. Code 58.1-802, paid by the seller unless the parties agree otherwise. The clerk of the circuit court collects it when the deed is recorded, with half going to the state and half to the city.

The Treasurer's page also shows what happens when tax stays unpaid. It announced an online-only public auction of two Norfolk parcels for unpaid real estate tax, held under Va. Code 58.1-3975 in June 2026, sold as is with a 15 percent buyer's premium. That is a reminder that delinquency can end in a forced sale.

What should a Norfolk owner with tax due do first?

Start by getting the real number. A payoff from the Treasurer beats an estimate from a bill that may be several months old.

  • Call the Treasurer's office or use the eBilling portal to confirm which quarters are open.
  • Ask the Assessor at 757-664-4732 how the current value was set if you think it is too high.
  • Ask the Department of Human Services at 757-823-1130 whether you qualify for real estate tax relief.
  • Tell the title company about any nuisance abatement lien, since the Treasurer collects those too.

If you want to skip repairs and showings, we can make a written cash offer on a Norfolk house as is, and the title company pays the tax from the proceeds.

More questions about Norfolk, VA Property Tax Guide

What is the Norfolk real estate tax due date?

Norfolk bills quarterly, with payments due September 30, December 5, March 31 and June 5. The Treasurer mails bills at least 30 days before each date. City Council sets the dates and rates each year, so check your current bill.

Who do I call about my Norfolk assessment?

Call the City Assessor's office at 757-664-4732 for questions about value. To schedule an informal appeal with an appraiser, call 757-823-1343 after your April notice arrives.

When is the Norfolk Board of Review deadline?

The city code says appeals go to the Board of Review by the last business day in May. Late appeals can still be heard by the assessor, but the Board will not take them until the following year. File one application per parcel with an original and five copies.

Can I sell a Norfolk house if I owe property tax?

Yes. Virginia puts the tax lien first, so the unpaid amount comes out of the sale proceeds at closing and the treasurer releases the lien. Ask for a payoff figure before you sign anything.

Does Norfolk have an auction for unpaid tax?

Yes. The Treasurer's page lists an online-only public auction of parcels with unpaid real estate tax, sold under Va. Code 58.1-3975. Selling before a parcel reaches that stage keeps you in control of the price and the timing.

Some bills combine the real estate tax with a stormwater fee, and the Treasurer's payment page tells online bankers to pay the grand total per account number.

How does a Newport News assessment appeal work?

Newport News uses a Board of Review that sits between September 1 and November 30 each year. Its city page says applications are accepted from July 1 through September 1, with no extensions.

  • Deadline: if September 1 falls on a weekend or holiday, the next business day applies.
  • Late filings: an application postmarked or hand delivered after the deadline is not accepted.
  • Mail warning: the page notes that since December 24, 2025, a USPS postmark reflects the processing date, which can be later than the day you mailed.
  • Who sits on it: the Newport News Circuit Court judges appoint the Board each year.
  • Where to ask: the Board's administrative assistant at 757-812-7816.

Separate forms exist for residential and commercial appeals. The same page links a procedures document for the 2026 cycle and a letter of authorization for agents.

Newport News sits at the southeastern end of the Virginia Peninsula, on the north shore of the James River where it meets Hampton Roads. Wikipedia lists 119.63 square miles in total, of which 69.00 are land and 50.63 are water, and an elevation of 15 feet.

The 2020 census counted 186,247 residents. The city was settled in 1691 and incorporated in 1896, and in 1958 voters in Warwick and Newport News chose to consolidate under the Newport News name. Several neighborhoods sit in what used to be the City of Warwick, so an address can have a different history than a neighbor a few miles away.

Climate is humid subtropical, with snowfall averaging 5.8 inches a season according to the same article. With 42 percent of the city's area made up of water, a seller should expect buyers to ask whether a house is near a creek, a river inlet or a mapped flood zone.

Which neighborhoods and employers shape the Newport News market?

Newport News has dozens of named neighborhoods, from the planned community of Hilton Village in the south to Denbigh in the north. Wikipedia also lists Oyster Point, City Center, Port Warwick, Lee Hall, Riverside, Menchville, Windsor Great Park and the East End, among others. Port Warwick and City Center at Oyster Point came from New Urbanism projects that began in the early 2000s.

Employment is tied to the water and the military. The article gives these figures for the largest employers:

  • Newport News Shipbuilding, owned by Huntington Ingalls Industries: over 24,000 employees.
  • Fort Eustis: over 10,000.
  • Newport News School System: over 5,000.
  • Thomas Jefferson National Accelerator Facility: over 675 staff.

Interstates 64 and 664 and the Monitor-Merrimac Memorial Bridge-Tunnel connect the city to the rest of Hampton Roads, and Newport News/Williamsburg International Airport is inside city limits.

What does the city's assessment ratio and tax base tell a seller?

The assessment history shows a 100 percent ratio every year, which means the city assesses at full value and applies the rate to that figure. Total taxable assessment for 2025-26 is $23,634,402,300, about 4.2 percent above the $22,686,862,600 listed for 2024-25.

The Assessor's page describes the work in plain terms: assess all real estate, administer the laws on assessments and exemptions, keep records on every parcel, publish an annual land book and review assessments with owners. If your value jumped, ask for that review before the September 1 appeal deadline arrives.

The Assessor does not set the rate or assessment policy. The FAQ says the rate comes from City Council and the tax equals assessed value times the rate, so a disagreement about the dollar amount is a conversation with Council, while a disagreement about value is an appeal.

What happens to tax owed when a Newport News house is sold?

Virginia law puts a tax lien on the real estate ahead of any other lien, so delinquent tax gets paid from the sale proceeds. Va. Code 58.1-3340 says the buyer, or the trustee at a foreclosure sale, must apply proceeds to taxes and levies, including penalties and interest, and the treasurer then releases the lien.

The statute says the seller's liability for the year is prorated by contract, so the sale agreement should say who pays the current half. Va. Code 58.1-802 adds a state and local grantor's tax of 50 cents per $500 of price, paid by the seller unless the parties arrange otherwise. The circuit court clerk collects it at recording.

The Treasurer also maintains a page for real estate auctions of properties with delinquent taxes or liens, and it posts the legal notice and auction flyer. An owner who sees a notice for their own parcel has little time left to choose the terms of a sale.

Are there relief programs for Newport News owners behind on tax?

Newport News lists several relief programs, and the Commissioner of the Revenue administers them. The city's search results show pages for a real estate tax deferral for the elderly and disabled, an exemption for disabled veterans and mobile home deferral and exemption programs.

It also lists a Residential Rehabilitation Property Tax Abatement Program with its own calculator, and a VA Deed Alert tool on the Assessor's site. Rules and income limits live on those pages, so we do not repeat them here. Call 757-926-8653 for state income and tax relief questions.

If a program does not fit and the house needs more work than you can fund, a cash sale of the property as is can clear the tax at closing instead.

They are normally due December 5 and June 5. The city's FAQ also notes that improvements to the land may be billed on a supplemental bill.

Applications to the Board of Review are accepted July 1 through September 1, and no extensions are granted. If September 1 is a weekend or holiday, the following business day is the deadline.

Who is the Newport News Treasurer and how do I reach the office?

The city lists the Treasurer's mailing address as P.O. Box 975, Newport News, VA 23607, with the phone 757-926-8731 and the email treasurer@nnva.gov. Office hours are Monday through Friday, 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM.

Yes. Virginia's tax lien comes first, so the title company pays the balance from your proceeds and the treasurer releases the lien. Ask for a written payoff amount before closing.

Richmond is the capital of Virginia, built at the fall line of the James River, and it had 226,610 residents at the 2020 census (Wikipedia).

Founded in 1737, Richmond replaced Williamsburg as the capital of the colony in 1780. Its economy runs on law, finance and government, with federal, state and local agencies and banking and legal firms downtown. The median age at the 2020 census was 32.4.

Shockoe Bottom is the low-lying area between Shockoe Hill and Church Hill. Carytown is a commercial strip along Cary Street, the Fan District and Oregon Hill are named neighborhoods, and the East End includes Church Hill, Fulton, Union Hill and Fairmount. Because Richmond is an independent city, one city government assesses, bills and collects the real estate tax, with no county layer.

We could not open the city's page on rates, penalties and interest, so we do not state them here. The city also posts an online penalty and interest waiver request form through RVA 311, and Finance can tell you what applies to your account.

How do I appeal a Richmond assessment?

Richmond lists three steps: office review, then the Board of Equalization, then a direct appeal to the court.

The assessor says notices go to each owner's last known address on or about July 1 and show the proposed assessment, prior values and the calculated change in tax. If you have questions, call the assessor's front desk at (804) 646-7500 and talk with the area appraiser before requesting a formal review (appeal process page). The page also lists a tool to determine your residential neighborhood. We could not read the individual deadlines for each step, so we do not list them.   • Check the recorded square footage, bedroom count and condition notes.

What is Richmond's real estate tax sale program?

It is the city's process for auctioning property with long-delinquent real estate tax, and the city says it will relaunch in November 2026 after a pause that began in January 2023.

A property becomes eligible when taxes have been delinquent for two full calendar years, or one year if the property is condemned, a nuisance, derelict or blighted, under Virginia Code 58.1-3965. The unpaid tax is paid from the sale proceeds, because Virginia gives real estate tax a lien ahead of any other lien.

Sellers with back taxes, tenants or a house needing repairs often compare a direct sale with listing. In both cases the tax payoff comes out of the proceeds.

What is the history of Hampton?

Hampton claims to be the oldest continuously occupied English settlement in the United States, with the colonists establishing a town and what is now St. John's Episcopal Church in 1610. It became a town in 1705, a city in 1849 and an independent city in 1908.

On July 1, 1952, the city of Hampton, the town of Phoebus and Elizabeth City County merged into one independent city after voters approved. That merger is why older Hampton records may mention Elizabeth City County.

Fort Monroe, at Old Point Comfort, was decommissioned as an army base on September 15, 2011 and named a national monument that November. Hampton University was founded after the Civil War across the Hampton River from the fort.

What jobs and institutions shape Hampton?

The federal presence is large. Langley Air Force Base, the nation's first military installation dedicated to air power, is in Hampton, and so is NASA's Langley Research Center.

Other anchors are Hampton University, Virginia Peninsula Community College, the Virginia Air and Space Science Center and the Hampton Coliseum. Wikipedia also notes a NASCAR short track and a long Navy and Air Force family presence.

Military assignments mean some Hampton owners move on short notice. A deployed or transferred owner who needs to sell may not have time for repairs and showings.

The city's neighborhoods include Aberdeen Gardens, Buckroe Beach, Farmington, Fox Hill, Hampton Woods, Northampton, Newmarket, Phoebus, the Victoria Boulevard Historic District and Wythe, which includes the Olde Wythe Historic District.

Historic district status can limit exterior changes, so a seller in Olde Wythe or Phoebus should ask city planning staff what applies to the address. We did not open an official page on district rules, so we do not summarize them here.

  • Old Hampton and Phoebus date to the colonial and 19th-century town centers.
  • Phoebus was its own town until the 1952 merger.

What does the climate mean for a Hampton house?

Hampton has a humid subtropical climate with hot, humid summers and mild winters. Wikipedia gives a mean annual temperature of 60.2 degrees Fahrenheit, about 47 inches of rain and about 6 inches of snow a year.

The highest temperature on record was 105.1 degrees on August 1, 1980. For a house, that means attention to roofs, gutters, crawl space moisture and air conditioning age. We did not open an official Hampton flood-zone page, so ask the city and your insurer about the address.

How do roads and transit affect Hampton homes?

Interstate 64 and Interstate 664 meet near the Hampton Coliseum. The Hampton Roads Bridge-Tunnel is on I-64 near downtown Hampton, and the Monitor-Merrimac Memorial Bridge-Tunnel is on I-664 nearby in Newport News.

U.S. routes 17, 60 and 258 and State Routes 134 and 143 also serve the city. The Hampton Transit Center at West Pembroke Avenue and King Street is a hub for Hampton Roads Transit buses, and Amtrak runs from the Newport News station.

Which schools serve Hampton?

Hampton City Public Schools runs four high schools, Kecoughtan, Bethel, Phoebus and Hampton, along with elementary, middle and specialty schools.

Zone boundaries depend on the address, so check with the division before quoting a school to a buyer.

Who bills and who assesses real estate tax in Hampton?

The City Assessor sets the value, and the Treasurer bills and collects. The assessor's office is at One Franklin Street, Suite 602, phone 757-727-8311. The Treasurer is at One Franklin Street, Suite 100, phone 757-727-6374.

The city says all real estate is appraised each year and assessed at 100 percent of market value, and that the real estate tax rate is $1.14 per $100 of assessed value. The tax year runs from July 1 to June 30.

Where is Suffolk, Virginia, and why is the city so large?

Suffolk is an independent city in the Hampton Roads region of southeastern Virginia, and it is the largest city in the state by land area. It covers 428.91 square miles, with 399.17 of them land and 29.74 water, at an elevation of 39 feet.

The size comes from a merger. The 2020 census counted 94,324 people, and the 2025 Census Bureau estimate is 104,699. Because the city spans farmland, swamp, small villages and a suburban north end, a house in one part of Suffolk can differ sharply from one in another.

What are Suffolk's seven boroughs?

Suffolk is divided politically into seven boroughs: Chuckatuck, Cypress, Holy Neck, Nansemond, Sleepy Hole, Suffolk and Whaleyville. The Suffolk borough matches the former city, and the other six match the six magisterial districts of the old Nansemond County.

Colonists founded Suffolk in 1742 as a port town on the Nansemond River, first called Constant's Warehouse. It was renamed for Suffolk in England, became an incorporated town in 1808, and became a city in 1910.

Railroads and later highways made it a transportation gateway east into South Hampton Roads. Peanuts then became the signature crop, and Planters' Peanuts was established here beginning in 1912. The company's founder Amedeo Obici and the Mr. Peanut mascot are part of local history, and the city has held its Peanut Fest every fall since 1977.

Suffolk is a peanut processing center, a rail and highway hub, and a home to defense contractors and distribution centers. The mix gives the city jobs in farming, logistics, manufacturing and technology.

The U.S. Joint Forces Command, which stood near U.S. 17 and Interstate 664, was disestablished in August 2011. Where is Chesapeake, Virginia, and how big is it?

Chesapeake is an independent city in the Hampton Roads area of southeastern Virginia. It borders Portsmouth and Norfolk to the north, Virginia Beach to the east, Suffolk to the west, and North Carolina's Currituck and Camden counties to the south.

The 2020 census counted 249,422 residents, making it the second most populous city in Virginia. By land area it is the second largest city in the state, with about 338.5 square miles of land and 12.4 square miles of water. Elevation is only 16 feet.

The modern city dates to 1963, when South Norfolk merged with what remained of Norfolk County, approved by referendum and authorized by the General Assembly. The Battle of Great Bridge was fought here on December 9, 1775.

What are Chesapeake's six boroughs and waterways?

The city is divided into six boroughs: South Norfolk, Butts Road, Deep Creek, Pleasant Grove, Western Branch and Washington. A house in each borough can feel very different, from dense older streets to large rural lots.

Water shapes the whole city. The northeastern part of the Great Dismal Swamp lies in Chesapeake, and the Great Dismal Swamp National Wildlife Refuge covers a large piece of it. The Atlantic Intracoastal Waterway passes through, along with the Western and Southern Branches of the Elizabeth River and the Dismal Swamp Canal, which runs parallel to U.S. Highway 17.

Humidity matters for houses. Crawl space moisture, attic ventilation and air conditioning load are typical items a buyer's inspector will raise, and a house with deferred upkeep can show those problems quickly.

The largest employers are the public schools (6,248), the City of Chesapeake (3,927), Chesapeake Regional Medical Center (2,038), Walmart (1,783) and Sentara Healthcare (1,478). Dollar Tree has its international headquarters here, and the Navy runs Northwest Annex and NALF Fentress.

  • Tolls: the Chesapeake Expressway on State Route 168, Veterans Bridge and Jordan Bridge.
  • Five movable bridges, which open an estimated 30,000 times a year.

Norfolk International Airport serves the city, and five railroads, including CSX and Norfolk Southern, run through it. A bridge opening can slow a commute, which is a detail buyers ask about.

Chesapeake values property as of January 1, and new values take effect July 1. Owners whose value changed are mailed a notice, and for the current cycle those notices go out on or before March 1, 2027.

New construction, additions and demolitions are picked up through supplemental bills, with valuation changes captured on October 1, January 1, April 1 and July 1. A teardown or an addition done before listing can therefore change the bill during the year.

The Assessor's office is at 306 Cedar Road, 4th Floor, with phone 757-382-6235 and email assessor@cityofchesapeake.net. A free property search is available at chesapeake.civ.quest, while the city's paid tax information subscription costs $1,100 a year or $100 a month.

For owners over 65 or disabled, the city runs tax relief through the Commissioner of the Revenue at 757-382-6455, option 4. Applications run from January 1 through May 15, and the city listed relief of 100 percent for household income up to $25,000 in fiscal year 2025. Check the current limits, because they are listed by year.

Chesapeake sellers should confirm four things: the current quarter's real estate tax, the stormwater fee, any land use enrollment and the recordation costs. Where is Lynchburg and how did it develop?

Lynchburg is an independent city on the James River in the foothills of the Blue Ridge Mountains, near the geographic center of Virginia. Wikipedia lists 49.53 square miles and an elevation of 630 feet, with 79,009 residents in the 2020 census and an estimate of 81,347 for 2025.

Tobacco, trade and later iron and steel manufacturing powered the early economy, and the James River and Kanawha Canal reached the town in 1840.

The river that built the town also flooded it. The article records floods in 1842, 1847, 1870 and 1877, and the floods of 1870 and 1877 destroyed the city's bridges. A house near the river deserves a closer look at drainage than one on a ridge.

Where is Petersburg, VA, and why does its history show up in property records?

Petersburg is an independent city 21 miles south of Richmond, at the fall line of the Appomattox River, with 33,458 residents at the 2020 census (Wikipedia).

The House of Burgesses ordered Fort Henry built in 1645, three settlements were joined as the Town of Petersburg in 1748, and an 1815 fire led to a rebuilt town that became a rail and industrial hub. By 1860 it was the second-largest city in Virginia. The 1864 to 1865 Siege of Petersburg, including the Battle of the Crater, devastated it, and parts of the battlefield are preserved as Petersburg National Battlefield.

Because Petersburg is an independent city, it has no county government above it. The city assessor values property, the Commissioner of the Revenue and Treasurer handle other taxes, and the city also runs the code office that enforces building rules. When are Petersburg real estate taxes due?

Petersburg bills real estate tax quarterly, and the assessor's page lists due dates of September 30, December 31, March 30 and June 30.

Petersburg reassesses every two years as of January 1, and it mails Change of Assessment Notices on January 28 of a reassessment year to owners whose value changed.

The assessor says all assessments are reviewed every two years even if not all change, using mass appraisal methods and the sales comparison, income and cost approaches. Appraisers work by assessment neighborhood and use the AssessPro computer-assisted mass appraisal system. They study recent sales first, and they may set aside sales that are not arm's-length, such as family transfers, foreclosures, bank sales, estate sales and other distressed sales tied to court orders or divorces.

For a seller, that means a discounted sale of a house, such as one from an estate, can be set aside when the assessor studies the market (assessment page). New construction and renovations are added when substantially complete and billed in a supplement for the part of the year they were finished.

  • Board of Equalization: appeals are due April 1 of the assessment year, or within 60 days of the notice date. The board has three members, owners with real estate backgrounds appointed by the circuit court judge.
  • Circuit Court: for owners unhappy with the board or who missed earlier deadlines. The city says there is no form and the filing is typically done by an attorney.

The assessor suggests calling and speaking with an appraiser before filing, and says the review is a chance to check the recorded square footage and features of your house. A request for income and expense data that goes unanswered can keep that data out of evidence later (appeals page). Virginia law also says the board starts from a presumption that the assessor's value is correct (Va. Code 58.1-3379).

  • Damage abatement: available if a building was unfit for use for 30 days or more and the loss cut its value by $500 or more. Apply within six months of the damage.
  • Land use: initial and annual applications are due May 1, with a $500 fee.

Under the city's vacant building registry, in Sec. 22-140 of the city code, an owner of a building continuously vacant for 12 months or more must register it with the building code official. The annual fee is $100, and the owner must describe how the building will be maintained and show a rodent abatement plan (registry page). A vacant house you plan to sell should be checked against this rule first.

The tax is paid out of the sale proceeds, because Virginia puts the real estate tax lien ahead of every other lien until it is paid.

The statute requires the purchaser, or the trustee in a foreclosure, to apply proceeds to taxes and levies, which include penalties and interest, and it says the seller's share is prorated by contract (Va. Code 58.1-3340). The deed also carries a grantor's tax of 50 cents per $500 of value, normally paid by the seller (Va. Code 58.1-802).

Sellers with back taxes, a vacant house, repairs they cannot fund or an inherited home often look at a direct sale. The closing agent still needs a payoff from the city, so call Billing and Collections before you sign a contract. An office review is due by March 1 of the assessment year or within 30 days of the notice. A Board of Equalization appeal is due by April 1 or within 60 days of the notice.

Charlottesville by the numbers

What kind of place is Charlottesville, Virginia?

Charlottesville is an independent city in central Virginia, on the Rivanna River, with Albemarle County all around it. It is the county seat of Albemarle, but the city and county are separate governments, and that matters for a property tax bill because only the city bills city addresses.

The city covers 10.27 square miles and had 46,553 residents in the 2020 census. It is about 99 miles from Washington, D.C., and 72 miles from Richmond, at an elevation of 594 feet.

Charlottesville was founded in 1762 and named for Queen Charlotte. Its historic center is Court Square, and its Downtown Mall is described as one of the longest outdoor pedestrian malls in the country.

How does the University of Virginia shape Charlottesville housing?

The University of Virginia is the largest force in the local housing picture. Its main grounds are on the city's west side, though most of the campus sits legally in Albemarle County, and more than 20,000 students come to the area in the academic year.

The biggest employers, each with over 1,000 workers, are UVA and its hospital, the UVA Health Services Foundation, the City of Charlottesville and the city school board. Crutchfield, Emerson Automation Solutions, PepsiCo and S&P Global are also listed. About 82 percent of people employed in the city commute in from elsewhere, so many workers hold a Charlottesville job and a house in another locality.

The text we read names Ridge Street, Fifeville, Tenth and Page, and Rose Hill as long-standing neighborhoods. Sellers in older streets near the university often own homes with age-related repair needs.

What is the weather like, and what does it mean for a Charlottesville house?

Charlottesville has a humid subtropical climate with four seasons. January averages 36.2 degrees Fahrenheit and July averages 77.6, and the city gets about 17 inches of snow in an average year.

That mix puts steady wear on roofs, gutters, older windows and heating systems. Record extremes run from minus 10 degrees in January 1994 to 107 in September 1954, so a house here can see both deep freezes and hot summers. A buyer's inspector will usually look hard at the roof and the heating equipment.

Which roads and trains reach Charlottesville?

Interstate 64 and U.S. Route 29 are the main highways. Charlottesville Union Station is served by Amtrak's Cardinal, Crescent and Northeast Regional routes, and the Charlottesville-Albemarle Airport serves the area.

Local transit includes Charlottesville Area Transit, JAUNT paratransit and University Transit Service. Homes with easy access to those routes and to downtown tend to draw more attention from buyers who commute without a car.

When are Charlottesville real estate taxes due and how much is the rate?

Charlottesville real estate tax is due in two equal installments, on June 5 and December 5, and the city lists a rate of $0.99 per $100 of assessed value. City Council sets the rate in the spring. If a deadline falls on a weekend, it moves to the following Monday.

ItemCity of Charlottesville
Due datesJune 5 and December 5
Rate$0.99 per $100 of assessed value
Late penalty10 percent of the tax due, the day after the deadline
Interest10 percent a year, accruing monthly
Treasurer phone434-970-3146
Mailing addressP.O. Box 2854, Charlottesville, VA 22902

A payment plan does not stop penalties and interest, according to the city. If the tax goes unpaid, the city lists bank account liens, rent liens and wage garnishments as collection methods, and says properties with three or more years of unpaid tax are subject to judicial sale. To ask for a penalty waiver, the city asks you to read its Late Payment Penalty Policy and write to the Treasurer with supporting documents.

How does the City Assessor value Charlottesville property?

The City Assessor values every parcel each year, as of January 1, and mails change of assessment notices at the end of January. Under city code, all real estate is assessed annually.

Most homes are valued by comparing recent sales of similar houses in the same neighborhood. The city says auctions, bank foreclosures, condemnations and transfers between family members generally do not count as arm's-length sales. That is useful to know if your house sold recently under unusual terms.

  • Office: 102 5th Street NE, Charlottesville, VA 22902, by appointment, phone 434-970-3136.
  • Mail: P.O. Box 911, Charlottesville, VA 22902.
  • Commissioner of the Revenue: 605 E Main Street, Room A-130, phone 434-970-3160.

Where can you look up Charlottesville property records?

The City Assessor keeps a history file for every parcel, with ownership, deed and plat references, ownership history and details of improvements. The city also publishes assessment neighborhood maps, land books and GIS data, and its GIS Viewer gives access to real estate records online. A public computer is available at the Assessor's office for the same purpose.

  • Assessment neighborhood maps and land books, posted on the city's assessor pages.
  • An Income and Expense form for income-producing property.
  • An Assessment Appeal Application form, which you can also request by phone.

Before you list, compare your record against the house itself. The city accepts factual discrepancies such as square footage, acreage or the condition of improvements as grounds for appeal, and a corrected record can lower the bill you pass to the next owner. If an agent files for you, include a Letter of Authorization.

How do you appeal a Charlottesville assessment?

Appeal in three steps: the assessor, the Board of Equalization, then Circuit Court. A high tax bill or a large jump in value is not enough by itself. The city accepts factual errors in the property record, uneven values within a neighborhood, and disagreements over fair market value.

  1. Call the appraiser at 434-970-3136 with your owner name, address or nine digit parcel ID. Many questions end here.
  2. File an Assessment Appeal Application with your reasoning and evidence. The appraiser may inspect the property and will mail a decision, which the city says comes within 30 days.
  3. Ask for a Board of Equalization review within 30 days of the decision letter. The board is an independent citizen panel appointed by the Circuit Court judge, and it mails its decision within 30 days after the hearing.
  4. As a last step, appeal to Circuit Court. You carry the burden of proof and pay court costs.

The city pages we opened do not give a filing deadline for the first application, so call the assessor's office to confirm it. Virginia law, in 58.1-3379, presumes the assessor's value is correct and requires the owner to rebut it with evidence.

What should Charlottesville sellers with unpaid tax know?

The main point is that the Treasurer's balance includes penalty and interest, so the payoff changes month to month. Ask the Treasurer at 434-970-3146 for a figure that matches your closing date.

The Commissioner of the Revenue lists tax relief programs for the elderly and disabled, a homeowner assistance program and an exemption for disabled veterans and surviving spouses. The page carries a note that the real estate relief program has ended, so confirm what is currently open before you count on it.

At closing, Virginia's grantor tax is 50 cents for each $500 of value under 58.1-802, normally paid by the seller. If your Charlottesville house needs work or has back tax, Cash Home Buyers can review it as is and plan around the payoff figure the Treasurer gives you.

More questions about Charlottesville, VA Property Tax Guide

When are Charlottesville real estate taxes due?

June 5 and December 5, in equal installments. A due date that lands on a weekend moves to the next Monday.

What is the Charlottesville real estate tax rate?

The city lists $0.99 per $100 of assessed value, set by City Council. Confirm the current rate with the Treasurer, since council sets it each spring.

How do I dispute my Charlottesville assessment?

Call the City Assessor at 434-970-3136, then file an Assessment Appeal Application. If you disagree with the decision, ask the Board of Equalization to review it within 30 days, and use Circuit Court as the final step.

What happens if Charlottesville property tax goes unpaid?

A 10 percent penalty applies the day after the deadline, and interest accrues at 10 percent a year. The city lists liens and wage garnishment, and judicial sale for three or more years of unpaid tax.

Can I sell a Charlottesville house with tax still due?

Yes, the balance is normally paid from proceeds at closing. Get a current payoff from the Treasurer's Office before the closing date.
